Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OB}} stands for {{c2::obstetrics}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "OB emergency, 38 weeks, crowning, requesting L&D on standby."
  2. Handoff: "G3P2 at 39 weeks, contractions 3 min apart, taking her to OB triage."
  3. Charting: "Third-trimester bleeding, transported to OB rather than the main ED."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OBS}} stands for {{c2::organic brain syndrome}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Nursing home pt with hx of OBS, family confirms baseline confusion."
  2. Handoff: "Per facility, her OBS is at baseline, no acute change in mentation."
  3. History: "Documented OBS, history obtained from caregiver since pt is a poor historian."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, OD can stand for {{c1::overdose, right eye, optical density, outside diameter, doctor of optometry}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As overdose: "opioid OD, pinpoint pupils, RR 6" — give naloxone; the toxicology emergency.
  2. As right eye: "instill 1 drop OD" — OD (oculus dexter) = right eye; OS = left, OU = both.
  3. As doctor of optometry: OD — the optometrist who does eye exams and refractions (vs an MD ophthalmologist).

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OP}} stands for {{c2::outpatient}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Stable pt, advised OP follow-up with PCP within 2 days."
  2. Discharge: "D/C home with OP cardiology referral for the palpitations."
  3. Handoff: "Minor lac, will be an OP suture removal, not getting admitted."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OPA}} stands for {{c2::oropharyngeal airway}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "No gag reflex, sized and inserted OPA, ventilating with BVM."
  2. Radio report: "Unresponsive OD, OPA placed, bagging at 100% O2, sats 94%."
  3. Handoff: "OPA tolerated with no gag, airway patent, good chest rise on BVM."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OR}} stands for {{c2::operating room}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "GSW to the abdomen, hypotensive, going straight to the OR."
  2. Charting: "Pt taken emergently to OR for exploratory laparotomy."
  3. Radio report: "Suspected ectopic rupture, have the OR on standby."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OS}} stands for {{c2::left eye}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Chemical splash to OS, irrigating with saline en route."
  2. Order: "2 gtt tetracaine OS prior to foreign body removal."
  3. Charting: "c/o foreign body sensation OS, OD unaffected."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::OU}} stands for {{c2::both eyes}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pt reports gradual blurred vision OU over the past week."
  2. Order: "Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment OU at bedtime."
  3. Charting: "Allergic conjunctivitis, itching and redness OU."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::oz}} stands for {{c2::ounce}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Infant took only 2 oz per feeding, fewer wet diapers today."
  2. Charting: "Reports drinking 24 oz of water hourly yet still thirsty."
  3. Charting: "Burn to anterior chest from a spilled 12 oz coffee."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::p̄}} stands for {{c2::after}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "SOB p̄ exertion, resolves with rest."
  2. Charting: "Vomiting p̄ meals for three days."
  3. Charting: "Lightheadedness p̄ standing, suggestive of orthostasis."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PA}} stands for {{c2::physician assistant}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Handing the laceration off to the PA in fast track."
  2. Charting: "Pt evaluated by PA, sutured and discharged with wound care."
  3. Charting: "PA reviewed the wrist X-ray, no fracture, splint applied."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::pc}} stands for {{c2::after meals}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Metformin 500 mg PO pc to reduce GI upset."
  2. Charting: "Home meds: antacid pc and at bedtime for reflux."
  3. Charting: "Pt checks fingerstick glucose pc, runs elevated."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PCO2}} stands for {{c2::partial pressure of carbon dioxide}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "ABG shows pH 7.28, PCO2 58, respiratory acidosis."
  2. Handoff: "COPD exacerbation with rising PCO2, may need BiPAP."
  3. Handoff: "Obtunded overdose, repeat ABG PCO2 68, intubating for hypercapnic respiratory failure."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, PE can stand for {{c1::pulmonary embolism, physical examination}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As pulmonary embolism: "sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia — rule out PE" — a clot lodged in the pulmonary artery; can kill fast.
  2. As physical examination: "on PE, lungs clear, abdomen soft" — findings from the hands-on exam (H&P).
  3. As pulmonary embolism: "leg DVT that embolized to a PE" — why immobile and post-op patients get clot prophylaxis.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PEARL or PERL}} stands for {{c2::pupils equal and reactive to light}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Neuro: PEARL, GCS 15, moving all four extremities."
  2. Charting: "Pupils PERL at 3 mm bilaterally."
  3. Handoff: "Head strike but PEARL and A&Ox4, denies LOC."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PEARLA}} stands for {{c2::pupils equal and reactive to light and accommodation}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Eyes: PEARLA, extraocular movements intact."
  2. Charting: "PEARLA bilaterally, no nystagmus noted."
  3. Handoff: "Postictal but pupils PEARLA, returning to baseline."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PEARRL}} stands for {{c2::pupils equal and round, regular in size, react to light}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pupils PEARRL at 4 mm with brisk response."
  2. Charting: "Neuro exam: PEARRL, face symmetric, grips equal."
  3. Handoff: "MVC with airbag deployment, PEARRL and neuro intact."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ped or peds}} stands for {{c2::pediatric}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Inbound with a peds respiratory distress, 4 y/o, activate the peds team."
  2. Charting: "Dosing per Broselow tape, peds arrest protocol initiated."
  3. Handoff: "Transferring the febrile 8-month-old to the peds ED."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PEEP}} stands for {{c2::positive end-expiratory pressure}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Set the vent PEEP to 5 and titrate to sats."
  2. Handoff: "ARDS patient, increased PEEP to recruit alveoli."
  3. Charting: "Applied PEEP valve to the BVM for pulmonary edema."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PERRL}} stands for {{c2::pupils equal, round, and reactive to light}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pupils PERRL at 3 mm, no anisocoria."
  2. Charting: "Neuro: PERRL, GCS 15, speech clear."
  3. Handoff: "Syncope workup, PERRL and neuro grossly intact."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PID}} stands for {{c2::pelvic inflammatory disease}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Lower abdominal pain with fever, r/o PID."
  2. Handoff: "Young female with cervical motion tenderness, concern for PID."
  3. Radio report: "Reproductive-age female, septic-appearing, query PID versus appendicitis."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PMH}} stands for {{c2::past medical history}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "PMH: HTN, T2DM, and CVA in 2021."
  2. Radio report: "68 y/o F, PMH of COPD, presenting with worsening SOB."
  3. Handoff: "No significant PMH, this is her first seizure."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PND}} stands for {{c2::paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "72 y/o with PND and orthopnea, JVD present, likely CHF."
  2. Charting: "Reports PND, waking short of breath x3 nights, now sleeps upright."
  3. Handoff: "Positive PND and bilateral edema, treating as heart failure."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::po}} stands for {{c2::per os (by mouth)}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Aspirin 324 mg po, have the pt chew it, for chest pain."
  2. Charting: "Tolerating fluids po without nausea or vomiting."
  3. Order: "Acetaminophen 650 mg po q6h PRN for fever."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PO}} stands for {{c2::postoperative, post-op}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "PO from a hip replacement this morning, first time out of bed."
  2. Charting: "PO CABG patient with new-onset AFib on the monitor."
  3. Radio report: "Interfacility transfer, immediate PO after appendectomy, stable."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PRN}} stands for {{c2::pro re nata (as needed)}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL PRN chest pain, hold if SBP under 100."
  2. Order: "Albuterol neb PRN wheezing."
  3. Order: "Ondansetron 4 mg IV PRN nausea."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::psi}} stands for {{c2::pounds per square inch}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Rig check: "Portable O2 reads 2000 psi, main tank 1800 psi."
  2. Rig check: "Portable's down to 500 psi, swap it before the next run."
  3. Charting: "O2 cylinder at 1500 psi at patient contact."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PSVT}} stands for {{c2::paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Regular narrow-complex tach at 190, looks like PSVT, trying vagals."
  2. Order: "Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push for the PSVT, flush after."
  3. Charting: "PSVT broke to sinus rhythm after second dose of adenosine."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::pt}} stands for {{c2::patient}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pt A&Ox4, denies chest pain or SOB."
  2. Charting: "On arrival, pt found tripoding and diaphoretic."
  3. Handoff: "Pt's a full code, spouse has the med list."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, PT can stand for {{c1::physical therapy, prothrombin time}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As prothrombin time: "PT/INR 5.8 on this warfarin patient with a GI bleed — reverse it now."
  2. As physical therapy: "Refer to PT for gait training after the total knee replacement."
  3. As prothrombin time: PT climbs in liver failure — the liver can't make its clotting factors.

Text: As a medical abbreviation, PTA can stand for {{c1::prior to admission, plasma thromboplastin antecedent}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As prior to admission: "Chest pain began about two hours PTA, per the patient."
  2. As prior to admission: "He was walking at baseline PTA, then suddenly collapsed."
  3. As plasma thromboplastin antecedent: the old name for clotting Factor XI; its deficiency causes hemophilia C.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PTT}} stands for {{c2::partial thromboplastin time}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Draw a baseline PTT before starting the heparin drip."
  2. Handoff: "On heparin, next PTT due at 1400."
  3. Charting: "PTT came back supratherapeutic, drip held per protocol."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, PVC can stand for {{c1::premature ventricular contraction, polyvinyl chloride}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As premature ventricular contraction: "Monitor shows frequent PVCs — early, wide beats; watch for runs of V-tach."
  2. As polyvinyl chloride: IV bags, tubing, and ET tubes are commonly molded from PVC plastic.
  3. As premature ventricular contraction: "Every other beat is a PVC — that's ventricular bigeminy on the strip."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::PVD}} stands for {{c2::peripheral vascular disease}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Hx of PVD; pedal pulses faint, feet cool and pale."
  2. Handoff: "Known PVD, so the mottled foot may be her baseline."
  3. Charting: "PVD pt with a non-healing ulcer on the great toe."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::q}} stands for {{c2::every}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Reassess vitals q5min while on the nitro drip."
  2. Order: "Albuterol neb q20min x3 for the asthma attack."
  3. Order: "Recheck blood glucose q1h after the D50."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, RA can stand for {{c1::rheumatoid arthritis, right atrium}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As rheumatoid arthritis: "PMH: RA on methotrexate — chronic autoimmune joint inflammation."
  2. As right atrium: a central line tip should sit near the SVC–RA junction.
  3. As rheumatoid arthritis: "RA flare today — warm, swollen knuckles in both hands."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, RAD can stand for {{c1::reactive airway disease, right axis deviation}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As reactive airway disease: "Wheezing toddler with RAD — start a duoneb and watch the work of breathing."
  2. As right axis deviation: "The 12-lead shows RAD — think right heart strain, RVH, or PE."
  3. As right axis deviation: lead I negative with aVF positive is the quick way to spot RAD.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RBC}} stands for {{c2::red blood cell}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Active GI bleed, 2 units of packed RBCs hung."
  2. Charting: "Urinalysis positive for RBCs, gross hematuria."
  3. Charting: "Low RBC count on the CBC, anemia workup started."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, Rh can stand for {{c1::Rhesus blood factor, rhodium}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As Rhesus blood factor: "Mom is O negative — Rh-negative, so she needs RhoGAM to protect the next pregnancy."
  2. As Rhesus blood factor: "Type is A positive — that's ABO group A, Rh positive."
  3. As rhodium: the periodic-table element symbol (atomic number 45), not a clinical term.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RLL}} stands for {{c2::right lower lobe of the lung}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Coarse crackles in the RLL, febrile, treating as pneumonia."
  2. Radio report: "Diminished breath sounds over the RLL with productive cough."
  3. Handoff: "Witnessed aspiration; watch the RLL, that's where it usually lands."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RLQ}} stands for {{c2::right lower quadrant of the abdomen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Pain started periumbilical, now localized to the RLQ, ?appendicitis."
  2. Charting: "RLQ tenderness with guarding and positive rebound."
  3. Handoff: "Max pain at McBurney's point in the RLQ, surgery consulted."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RN}} stands for {{c2::registered nurse}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Bedside report given to the receiving RN in room 4."
  2. Charting: "Care transferred to the triage RN, belongings with pt."
  3. Handoff: "Flight RN assumed care on the helipad."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::R/O}} stands for {{c2::rule out}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "72 y/o M, crushing substernal chest pain; R/O acute MI, 12-lead obtained."
  2. Charting: "Sudden thunderclap headache, worst of life; transport to R/O subarachnoid bleed."
  3. Charting: "RLQ pain with fever and anorexia; kept NPO to R/O appendicitis."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, ROM can stand for {{c1::range of motion, rupture of membranes}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As range of motion: "Shoulder has full active ROM but pain at the end range."
  2. As rupture of membranes: "SROM at 39 weeks — clear fluid, contractions every four minutes."
  3. As range of motion: "Passive ROM exercises keep joints from stiffening in a bedbound patient."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RUL}} stands for {{c2::right upper lobe of the lung}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Diminished breath sounds in RUL with focal crackles on auscultation."
  2. Charting: "CXR shows RUL infiltrate, treating as pneumonia, sats 90%."
  3. Handoff: "Aspiration event while supine, RUL involved, watching for pneumonitis."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::RUQ}} stands for {{c2::right upper quadrant of the abdomen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Sharp RUQ pain after a fatty meal, positive Murphy's sign."
  2. Radio report: "RUQ tenderness with guarding, suspect acute cholecystitis."
  3. Handoff: "RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder, ultrasound ordered for gallstones."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Rx}} stands for {{c2::prescription}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Home Rx list: metoprolol, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metformin."
  2. Order: "New Rx: amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID x10 days."
  3. Handoff: "Out of albuterol inhaler, needs an Rx refill before discharge."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::s̄}} stands for {{c2::without}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Chest pain s̄ radiation and s̄ associated SOB."
  2. Handoff: "Resting comfortably s̄ distress at this time."
  3. Charting: "Abdomen soft s̄ tenderness, rebound, or guarding."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SaO2}} stands for {{c2::oxygen saturation}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "ABG: SaO2 90% with PaO2 60 on room air, starting supplemental O2."
  2. Handoff: "Repeat ABG SaO2 88% despite high-flow, escalating to BiPAP."
  3. Charting: "SpO2 reads 98% but co-oximetry SaO2 only 82% in CO poisoning."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SC}} stands for {{c2::subcutaneous}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily for DVT prophylaxis."
  2. Charting: "Insulin lispro 6 units SC given before the meal."
  3. Order: "Heparin 5,000 units SC q8h while non-ambulatory."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SG}} stands for {{c2::supraglottic}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Failed intubation x2, placed SG airway with good chest rise."
  2. Charting: "SG airway inserted, placement confirmed by waveform capnography."
  3. Handoff: "Arrived with SG airway in place, ED to assess for a definitive tube."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SICU}} stands for {{c2::surgical intensive care unit}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Post-op open AAA repair, going to SICU for overnight monitoring."
  2. Charting: "Admitted to SICU following exploratory laparotomy."
  3. Handoff: "Transferring the intubated trauma patient from the ED to the SICU."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SIDS}} stands for {{c2::sudden infant death syndrome}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "2-month-old found apneic and pulseless in crib, unwitnessed; concern for SIDS."
  2. Handoff: "Infant arrest, prone sleep position noted, SIDS vs other cause."
  3. Radio report: "Working an infant cardiac arrest, unknown down time, possible SIDS."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SL}} stands for {{c2::sublingual}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL q5min x3, hold if SBP <100."
  2. Charting: "0.4 mg nitro SL given, chest pain down from 8/10 to 3/10."
  3. Handoff: "Took 2 of his own SL nitro before arrival with partial relief."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SOB}} stands for {{c2::shortness of breath}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "63 y/o M c/o SOB on exertion x3 days, worse at night."
  2. Radio report: "Severe SOB, sats 89% RA, bilateral wheezes, placing on oxygen."
  3. Handoff: "SOB much improved after CPAP, sats now 95%."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SpO2}} stands for {{c2::saturation of peripheral oxygen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "SpO2 96% on room air, no distress, lungs clear."
  2. Radio report: "SpO2 84% on arrival, up to 93% on 15 L NRB."
  3. Handoff: "SpO2 reading low with poor waveform, moving the probe to a better site."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::S/S, S&S}} stands for {{c2::signs and symptoms}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "S/S of acute stroke: facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech."
  2. Handoff: "S&S of hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, confusion) resolved after oral glucose."
  3. Charting: "No S/S of shock; skin warm and dry, cap refill <2 sec."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::stat}} stands for {{c2::immediately}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Get a stat 12-lead EKG and notify the physician."
  2. Order: "Stat portable chest X-ray for acute respiratory distress."
  3. Charting: "Stat glucose obtained: 38 mg/dL, D50 administered."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::STEMI}} stands for {{c2::ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Anterior STEMI on the 12-lead, activating the cath lab, ETA 8 minutes."
  2. Charting: "62 y/o M crushing chest pain, ECG shows STEMI with ST elevation in II, III, aVF."
  3. Handoff: "STEMI alert called from the field, gave ASA 324 and started nitro drip."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::STI}} stands for {{c2::sexually transmitted infection}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "24 y/o F c/o dysuria and discharge, denies known STI exposure."
  2. History: "Pt reports STI screening last month, results pending, new partner since."
  3. Handoff: "Lower abd pain, ?PID from untreated STI, referred to ED for pelvic exam."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::subcut}} stands for {{c2::subcutaneous}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily for DVT prophylaxis."
  2. Charting: "Pt self-administered subcut insulin this AM but skipped breakfast."
  3. Handoff: "Gave subcut sumatriptan for her migraine, pain now down to a 2."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::SVT}} stands for {{c2::supraventricular tachycardia}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Narrow-complex SVT at 190, stable, attempting vagal maneuvers."
  2. Order: "SVT unresponsive to vagal, give adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push."
  3. Charting: "Pt converted from SVT to sinus rhythm after adenosine, rate now 88."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::sym or Sx}} stands for {{c2::symptoms}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pt reports Sx of nausea and diaphoresis prior to onset of chest pain."
  2. History: "Flu-like Sx x3 days, now febrile with productive cough."
  3. Handoff: "Stroke Sx resolved en route, likely TIA, still transporting for workup."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::T}} stands for {{c2::temperature}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Vitals: T 101.8, HR 104, BP 128/76, RR 20, SpO2 98%."
  2. Handoff: "Pt febrile with T of 39.1 rectal, gave acetaminophen at 1400."
  3. Radio report: "Elderly female, altered, T reads 95.2, treating for hypothermia."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::tab}} stands for {{c2::tablet}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Aspirin 324 mg, four 81 mg baby tabs, chewed for chest pain."
  2. Charting: "Pt took one nitro tab SL at home before EMS arrival, no relief."
  3. History: "Reports missing his lisinopril, down to two tabs left in the bottle."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::TB}} stands for {{c2::tuberculosis}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pt c/o night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis; r/o active TB."
  2. Handoff: "Placed pt in a mask, possible TB exposure, isolate on arrival."
  3. History: "Recent immigrant, positive TB skin test, currently on RIPE therapy."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, TBA can stand for {{c1::to be admitted, to be announced}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As to be admitted: "ED board shows three patients TBA tonight, all worked up and just holding for inpatient beds."
  2. As to be announced: "Surgery start time is TBA until an OR opens up."
  3. As to be admitted: "Bed 4 is a rule-out MI, TBA to cardiology once a telemetry bed opens."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::tech}} stands for {{c2::technician, technologist}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "ED tech is drawing labs and getting the pt on the monitor now."
  2. Charting: "Rad tech took the pt for a noncontrast head CT."
  3. Handoff: "Lab tech called a critical potassium of 6.8 on the last draw."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::TIA}} stands for {{c2::transient ischemic attack}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Facial droop and slurred speech that resolved, treating as TIA vs stroke."
  2. Charting: "71 y/o M with transient R arm weakness x15 min, now resolved, ?TIA."
  3. History: "Prior TIA last year, on aspirin and atorvastatin since."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::tid/t.i.d./TID}} stands for {{c2::three times a day}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Amoxicillin 500 mg PO tid x10 days for the ear infection."
  2. History: "Pt takes metformin 500 mg tid with meals for type 2 diabetes."
  3. Charting: "Reports using albuterol inhaler tid over the last two days for wheezing."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Tx}} stands for {{c2::treatment}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Initiated hypoglycemia Tx with oral glucose, mental status now improving."
  2. Charting: "Pt refused further Tx and transport, signed AMA after full explanation."
  3. History: "Recent Tx for CHF exacerbation, discharged on new dose of furosemide."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::UA}} stands for {{c2::urinalysis}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Get a clean-catch UA and CBC for this febrile, confused elderly pt."
  2. Handoff: "UA came back positive for nitrites and leuks, likely a UTI driving the AMS."
  3. Charting: "Flank pain with hematuria on UA dipstick, ?kidney stone."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::UE}} stands for {{c2::upper extremity}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT

  2. Radio report: "Facial droop with L UE weakness, positive stroke screen, ETA 6."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::URI}} stands for {{c2::upper respiratory infection}}.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::UTI}} stands for {{c2::urinary tract infection}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT

  2. Radio report: "Febrile elderly female, altered, concern for urosepsis from a UTI."

WHEN YOU'D USE IT

Text: The {{c1::word root}} is the foundation of a medical term — its main part or stem, carrying the core meaning.
Back Extra:
Ex: in cardiology, cardi (heart) is the root.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. cardi/o = heart — the stem inside cardiac, cardiology, and pericarditis; the part that stays constant and carries the core meaning while prefixes and suffixes just modify it.
  2. gastr/o = stomach — the root in gastritis, gastroscopy, and gastroenteritis; find the root and you know the word is about the stomach.
  3. nephr/o = kidney — the foundation of nephrology and nephrotic; the suffix names the action, the root names the subject.

Text: A {{c1::prefix}} is attached to the {{c2::beginning}} of a term and generally describes {{c3::location and intensity}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a suffix attaches to the END of the word.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. Tachy-cardia vs. brady-cardia — same root (heart); only the front prefix flips it fast vs. slow. Intensity lives up front.
  2. Sub-lingual — sub- (under) at the beginning fixes the location: under the tongue, where nitroglycerin dissolves.
  3. Hyper-tension — hyper- (excessive) leads off and marks the severity: elevated blood pressure.

Text: A {{c1::suffix}} is attached to the {{c2::end}} of a term and usually indicates a {{c3::procedure, condition, disease, or part of speech}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a prefix attaches to the BEGINNING of the word.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. Appendic-itis — the ending -itis (inflammation) names the disease; the suffix is what makes it a condition.
  2. Append-ectomy — swap the ending to -ectomy (excision) and now it names the procedure to remove it.
  3. Cardi-ac — the ending -ac (pertaining to) just changes the part of speech, turning the root 'heart' into an adjective.

Text: A {{c1::combining vowel}} connects a word root to a suffix or to another word root, and is usually the vowel {{c2::o}} — sometimes i or e instead.
Back Extra:
Ex: in gastroenterology, the two o's are combining vowels.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. cardi/o + -logy → cardiology — the o links root (heart) to suffix (study of); without it the word is unsayable.
  2. electr/o + cardi/o + -gram → electrocardiogram — two o's chain three parts into the ECG you run on chest pain (root to root to suffix).
  3. therm/o + -meter → thermometer — the o joins root (heat) to suffix (measure); the vowel is almost always o.

Text: A combining vowel is used between a word root and a suffix when the suffix begins with a {{c1::consonant}}, to make the term easier to pronounce.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: drop the combining vowel when the suffix begins with a vowel (eg, gastr + -itis = gastritis).

HOW IT WORKS
  1. arthr/o + -scopy → arthroscopy — -scopy starts with a consonant, so the o stays; compare arthr-itis, where the vowel-suffix drops it.
  2. cardi/o + -megaly → cardiomegaly — -megaly begins with m, so keep the o: the enlarged heart you'd see on a chest X-ray.
  3. neur/o + -pathy → neuropathy — -pathy begins with p, so the o stays: the nerve damage of a long-term diabetic.

Text: When a term has two word roots, a combining vowel is kept between them even when the second root {{c1::begins with a vowel}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: gastr/o/enter/o/logy keeps the o between gastr and enter.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. gastr/o + enter/o → gastroenteritis — enter/o starts with a vowel (e), yet the o between the two roots is kept.
  2. oste/o + arthr/o → osteoarthritis — arthr/o starts with a vowel (a), but the linking o stays: the wear-and-tear joint disease.
  3. electr/o + encephal/o → electroencephalogram — encephal/o starts with e, and the o holds: the EEG that reads brain activity.

Text: Medical plural endings: singular {{c1::-a}} → -ae; {{c2::-is}} → -es; {{c3::-ex or -ix}} → -ices; {{c4::-on or -um}} → -a; {{c5::-us}} → -i.
Back Extra:
Ex: vertebra→vertebrae; diagnosis→diagnoses; appendix→appendices; bacterium→bacteria; alveolus→alveoli.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. vertebra → vertebrae — -a becomes -ae: one spinal bone vs. the whole column you immobilize.
  2. embolus → emboli — -us becomes -i: one traveling clot vs. the shower that lodges in the lungs (PE).
  3. diagnosis → diagnoses — -is becomes -es: how a chart lists more than one at once.

Text: A patient sitting upright is placed in the {{c1::Fowler}} position.
Back Extra:
Cue: think of raising the head of the bed or stretcher.

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. CHF with pulmonary edema: sit them bolt upright (Fowler) — lying flat floods the lungs and worsens the SOB.
  2. Asthma or COPD attack: the patient's already tripoding to breathe; Fowler matches it and eases the work of breathing.
  3. Protecting the airway: keep an alert, nauseated or at-risk patient upright in Fowler to cut aspiration risk.

Text: The {{c1::semi-Fowler}} position reclines a patient to about {{c2::45°}}, while {{c1::high-Fowler}} sits them at about {{c2::90°}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the higher the Fowler name, the more upright the patient.

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Mild SOB, stable: semi-Fowler (~45°) eases breathing without laying them flat; ramp to high-Fowler (~90°) if distress climbs.
  2. Abdominal pain: semi-Fowler at ~45° with knees flexed relaxes the abdominal wall better than lying flat.
  3. Severe distress or CHF: don't stop halfway — go high-Fowler (~90°), fully upright, to maximize lung expansion.
